text: Bugs - All Things Product Podcast with Teresa Torres & Petra Wille Our Courses Train Your Team Articles Just Now Possible Get in Touch Sign in Subscribe Bugs - All Things Product Podcast with Teresa Torres & Petra Wille Teresa Torres 24 Nov 2026 12 min Listen to this episode on: Spotify | Apple Podcasts In a world of AI products, what even counts as a “bug” — and can you still promise to fix it? Petra Wille and Teresa Torres take on a word that’s quietly breaking down in the age of AI: the bug. With deterministic code, a bug is black and white — the software either does what was specified or it doesn’t. But as Teresa builds AI products (through her partnership with Vistaly on AI interview snapshots and opportunity solution trees), she keeps hitting a murkier reality: an agent’s output isn’t right or wrong so much as better or worse, and “good enough” turns out to be the hardest bar of all. They dig into why you can’t fix AI bugs one at a time — the trap of overfitting — and why the real work is reducing whole categories of errors through error analysis and evals. Teresa’s metaphor for the whole endeavor: building AI products is like steering a chaotic monster — and you want it to stay a monster. Key Takeaways “Bug” is getting fuzzy. With AI, outputs are better or worse rather than right or wrong, so whether something even is a bug becomes subjective. The real work is defining “good” — often across multiple dimensions (e.g., an email’s tone, length, and fit for the recipient) — and then the harder question of “good enough.” Beware overfitting: patching the prompt for every single complaint (“never use em dashes”) makes the agent brittle and worse at cases it hasn’t seen. You fix categories of bugs, not individual ones — collecting enough instances, running error analysis, and reducing error rates, which takes time and patience. Building AI products is like steering a chaotic monster: you can guide it onto the path and keep it there, but you’ll never make every error disappear — and you want it to keep some room to maneuver. Quality is still controllable — non-deterministic doesn’t mean uncontrollable. You just can’t expect perfect; you aim for good enough. This demands more collaboration — not just within the product team, but across sales, support, and the whole org — to share a concept of “good enough” and reset the expectation that every bug gets fixed. Notable Moments “With AI products, what’s a bug is a little more subjective.” — Teresa “Good enough is the hardest one.” — Teresa “If you change your prompt for every single error that’s reported, you start to create an agent. It’s very brittle.” — Teresa “Building AI products is like trying to steer a chaotic monster.” — Teresa “We don’t fix them, we only improve. We steer the monster.” — Petra Resources & Links: Follow Teresa Torres: https://ProductTalk.org Follow Petra Wille: https://Petra-Wille.com Mentioned in this episode: Vistaly — Teresa’s build partner on AI interview snapshots and AI opportunity solution trees, and the source of these real-world “bug” examples Vistaly’s AI is built by the creator of the opportunity solution tree Related episodes — the earlier conversations on AI evals and “defining what good looks like,” which this one builds directly on Concepts worth a look: overfitting , error analysis , evals , and deterministic vs. non-deterministic (agentic) systems Join the Conversation: Have thoughts on this episode?
